problemText: In the line "conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal," Lincoln develops his opening claim about the nation primarily through which method — and to what end?
choices: cause-effect — showing that the Civil War itself was directly caused by the precise wording of this one clause
definition — pinning down the nation's founding identity as a commitment to an idea (equality), rather than merely a date or place, so the rest of the speech can build on that redefinition
narration — recounting, as a continuous story, each individual founding father's personal decision to include this clause
comparison-contrast — measuring the new nation directly against a specific rival nation founded on different principles
hints: A method of development is HOW an idea gets built out, not just what the idea says.
Ask what this clause is doing: telling a story, tracing a cause, comparing two things, or pinning down what the nation fundamentally IS.

problemText: Swift opens his proposal not with his solution but with this scene: "the streets, the roads, and cabbin-doors crowded with beggars of the female sex, followed by three, four, or six children, all in rags." This method of development is best described as —
choices: narration — telling, in strict chronological order, the personal life story of one specific named beggar family
definition — formally defining the legal term "beggar" as it was used in Irish law of the period
cause-effect — tracing, step by step, the specific historical causes of the famine that produced this poverty
description — using concrete visual detail of a crowded, ragged street scene to make the abstract problem of poverty vividly felt before any solution is proposed
hints: Notice how much physical, visual detail is packed into this single sentence before Swift states any claim.
Ask which method makes an abstract problem 'felt' through the senses rather than argued through logic or story.

problemText: Henry opens his speech, "it is natural to man to indulge in the illusions of hope. We are apt to shut our eyes against a painful truth." As an introduction, this opening move primarily —
choices: frames the entire speech as a corrective to comforting illusions, signaling that Henry's aim is to force the delegates to face an unwelcome truth rather than cling to hope
apologizes in advance for the emotional tone Henry is about to adopt for the remainder of his remarks
summarizes, point by point, the specific terms of the peace proposal the delegates are about to vote on
concedes that Henry himself has, until this moment, shared in the delegates' hopeful view of reconciliation
hints: An introduction's job is to frame how everything that follows should be read — ask what stance this opening establishes.
What does Henry warn hope will do to those who indulge in it, and how does that warning set up the rest of the speech?

problemText: Lincoln closes, "that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth." As a conclusion, this closing line primarily —
choices: resolves a specific factual question about the exact number of soldiers who died at Gettysburg
redirects listeners away from the war entirely toward a discussion of postwar reconstruction policy
universalizes the sacrifice at this one battlefield into a stake in the survival of self-government everywhere, rather than merely closing out a funeral tribute
restates, without elaboration, the same idea already fully explained in the speech's opening sentence
hints: A strong conclusion often pushes a specific, local case toward a larger, universal principle.
Ask what this line claims is at stake beyond just this one battlefield and this one funeral.

problemText: Douglass opens by asking, "why am I called upon to speak here to-day?" instead of offering a direct statement of thanks. As an introduction, this opening question primarily —
choices: simply requests that the event's organizers clarify, for procedural reasons, why he specifically was chosen over another speaker
reassures the audience that Douglass fully shares their patriotic pride in the day being celebrated
announces, as a matter of scheduling, that Douglass's remarks will be brief given the lateness of the invitation
frames the entire speech around Douglass's own doubtful standing, previewing that what follows will interrogate rather than celebrate the occasion
hints: Ask why a public speaker would open by questioning his own right to be speaking at all.
This opening sets the lens for everything that follows — does it read as gratitude, or as doubt?

problemText: Swift describes the children as "a very great additional grievance" and admits past projectors were "grossly mistaken in their computation." Word choices like "grievance" and "computation" cluster together to build which tone?
choices: a warm, sentimental tone that dwells lovingly on the emotional bond between mothers and children
a detached, clinical, bureaucratic tone that treats a human crisis as a matter of paperwork and arithmetic
a furious, accusatory tone that directly blames named government officials for the crisis
a playful, joking tone that signals from the outset that none of the proposal should be taken seriously
hints: 'Grievance' and 'computation' both belong to the vocabulary of paperwork and ledgers, not of feeling.
Ask what kind of speaker reaches for these particular words to describe starving children.

problemText: Swift calls a year-old child "a most delicious nourishing and wholesome food." Applied to this subject, this diction most clearly produces which effect?
choices: a sincere culinary review, meant literally as helpful advice for parents seeking better nutrition
an earnest, appreciative tone that signals Swift's genuine approval of the practice he is describing
an ironic clash between calm, appetizing word choice and a monstrous subject, forcing the reader to supply the horror the flat tone withholds
a neutral scientific description meant only to establish the nutritional content of the meat in question
hints: Ask whether a reasonable person could actually mean these words literally about this subject.
Irony through diction works by mismatch — what's mismatched between the tone here and what's being described?

problemText: Henry warns that false hope makes listeners "listen to the song of that siren till she transforms us into beasts." This diction primarily creates a tone of —
choices: alarm — casting comforting hope as a seductive force that degrades reason and dignity if indulged
nostalgia — fondly recalling old myths that Henry heard in his own childhood education
gratitude — thanking the delegates for their optimism about the prospects of peace
amusement — poking gentle fun at delegates who enjoy classical literature too much
hints: A siren's song is deadly precisely because it sounds pleasant — map that onto what Henry says hope will do.
Ask what 'transforms us into beasts' suggests about the cost of giving in to that song.

problemText: Douglass first says, "Would to God, both for your sakes and ours, that an affirmative answer could be truthfully returned to these questions!" and later declares, "This Fourth of July is yours, not mine." How do these two moments connect in Douglass's line of reasoning?
choices: The first flatly contradicts the second, so the two statements cancel each other out and reveal a real inconsistency in the argument
The first and second are unrelated observations about two entirely separate topics, connected only by their shared location in the speech
The first restates a fact already proven earlier, and the second merely repeats that same fact in different words
The first briefly concedes what Douglass wishes were true, so that the second statement can turn against that wish and expose it as false, sharpening the accusation that follows
hints: Ask whether the first statement is something Douglass actually believes, or something he wishes were true.
Look for the pivot: what happens to the wish once Douglass turns to what is actually the case?

problemText: Lincoln moves through three claims: the dead "have consecrated" the ground; therefore "it is for us the living... to be dedicated... to the unfinished work"; so that the nation "shall have a new birth of freedom." How do these three stages connect in Lincoln's line of reasoning?
choices: Each stage restates the one before it in different words, so the passage is a single claim repeated three times rather than an actual chain

The soldiers' sacrifice already accomplished something words cannot (stage one); that fact obligates the living to finish their unfinished work (stage two); completing that work is what will produce a "new birth of freedom" (stage three) — each stage depends on the one before it
The three moments describe three unrelated audiences — the dead, the living delegates, and a future generation not yet born — with no logical connection between them
The passage abandons its claim about consecration and instead pivots to an entirely new argument about upcoming elections
hints: Ask what obligation stage one creates, and what stage two claims we owe because of it.
A line of reasoning means each stage depends on the one before — check whether removing stage one would still make stage three make sense.

problemText: In the line "We have petitioned; we have remonstrated; we have supplicated; we have prostrated ourselves before the throne," Henry develops his claim that peaceful means are exhausted primarily through which method — and to what end?
choices: definition — formally defining the legal term "petition" as it was specifically understood under British parliamentary procedure of that period
narration — recounting, in sequence, each peaceful measure already attempted, so their cumulative failure justifies what comes next
comparison-contrast — measuring the colonists' actions against a specific rival nation's own diplomatic history and precedent
description — using vivid physical detail of the throne room's architecture and furnishings to evoke its grandeur for the audience
hints: Count the sequence of past-tense verbs Henry stacks in a row.
Ask what this recounted sequence is building toward, rather than what any single verb means on its own.

problemText: In the line "above your national, tumultuous joy, I hear the mournful wail of millions," Douglass develops his claim primarily through which method — and to what end?
choices: definition — formally defining what qualifies as a national holiday under the era's prevailing law and custom
narration — recounting, in strict chronological order, the specific events of the day's festivities as they unfolded
comparison-contrast — juxtaposing the audience's celebratory joy against the enslaved's grief so the day's meaning fractures depending on who hears it
exemplification — offering an isolated real-world case study drawn from one enslaved family's own personal history
hints: Notice the two feelings placed side by side in one sentence: 'joy' above, 'wail' beneath.
Ask what this juxtaposition does to a single day's meaning, depending on who is listening.

problemText: Swift opens his proposal with a description of "streets, the roads, and cabbin-doors crowded with beggars," rather than his solution. As an introduction, this opening primarily —
choices: requests that Parliament immediately investigate the specific causes of rural poverty before any policy is proposed to address it
frames the entire proposal as a response to a real, visible crisis, so that whatever solution follows will be measured against this vivid scene of need
summarizes, in full and exhaustive legal detail, the specific poor-relief statutes and workhouse regulations already in effect across the kingdom at that time
apologizes in advance for the considerable length of the pamphlet that is about to follow this opening description
hints: An introduction's job is to frame how everything that follows should be read.
Ask what problem this opening scene establishes before any proposal is offered.

problemText: Douglass calls the celebration "a thin veil to cover up crimes which would disgrace a nation of savages." Word choices like "crimes" and "disgrace" cluster together to build which tone?
choices: a wistful, nostalgic tone that longs for a version of the holiday that no longer exists
an admiring tone that praises the nation's founders for their foresight
a neutral, journalistic tone that simply reports the day's events without judgment
a scathing, accusatory tone that frames the celebration itself as criminal concealment
hints: 'Crimes' and 'disgrace' both belong to the vocabulary of wrongdoing, not celebration.
Ask what kind of speaker reaches for these particular words to describe a national holiday.

problemText: Swift first names poor children as "a very great additional grievance," and later claims his proposal will make them "a common good to the publick." How do these two moments connect in Swift's line of reasoning?
choices: The first names children as a burden so that the second can resolve that named burden, making the proposal appear to answer a problem Swift has already established
The first and second are unrelated observations about two wholly separate topics raised elsewhere in the pamphlet
The first restates a claim already fully proven earlier in the pamphlet, and the second merely repeats that same claim
The first flatly contradicts the second in a way that reveals an unresolved inconsistency running through the whole of Swift's entire argument here
hints: Ask what problem the first phrase sets up, and what the second phrase claims to solve.
A line of reasoning has each stage depend on the one before it — check what would be lost if the first phrase were cut.

problemText: Henry first states "we have done everything that could be done to avert the storm" and later asks, "Shall we gather strength by irresolution and inaction?" How do these two moments connect in Henry's line of reasoning?
choices: The first and second address two wholly unrelated audiences seated within the very same assembly hall
The first restates a fact already proven earlier, and the second merely repeats that same fact in slightly different words
The first establishes that peaceful measures are exhausted, so the second question forecloses delay as a remaining option, pushing the assembly toward action
The first flatly contradicts the second in Henry's own speech here, so the two statements cancel out entirely and expose an inconsistency in his line of reasoning
hints: Ask what options remain once the first statement is accepted as true.
A line of reasoning means the second stage depends on the first — check what the question forecloses.
